summary: Defines a certificate profile, building on RFC 3280, for identity certificates issued to natural persons, called Qualified Certificates. It sets conventions for such certificates without defining legal requirements, so it is usable independent of local law. It obsoletes RFC 3039.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a template for digital ID cards for real people, so that different countries can make cards that look and work alike.

questions: how does rfc 3739 differ from rfc 3039
what attributes go in a qualified certificate subject
subtitle: A profile for X.509 identity certificates issued to real people, written to work under any country's legal rules.

tldr.problem: Identity certificates for natural persons, including those that meet legal rules for electronic signatures, need uniform names, key usage settings, biometric data and statements, which the general Internet certificate profile in RFC 3280 does not cover.
tldr.mechanism: The profile fixes which name attributes issuer and subject fields use, sets rules for several extensions, and adds two new ones: biometric information and qualified certificate statements.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3039 and lets a CA mark a certificate as a Qualified Certificate without defining any legal requirements itself. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3739 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 3039.

sections.title: Introduction and Changes Since RFC 3039
sections.content:
RFC 3739 is a certificate profile: it narrows the general X.509 format and the Internet profile in RFC 3280 for one purpose, identity certificates issued to natural persons. Implementers are required to consult RFC 3280 for the underlying formats and semantics.

It obsoletes RFC 3039. The changes include editorial clarifications that the profile applies to a broad type of certificates, support for the domainComponent and title attributes in subject names, removal of postalAddress, removal of title from the subject directory attributes extension, and fewer constraints on key usage settings. A new qualified certificate statement for this second version is defined, and the one for RFC 3039 is kept for backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second version of a rulebook for digital ID cards. It fixes a few rules from the first version and keeps a way to recognise old cards.

sections.title: What a Qualified Certificate Is
sections.content:
The term Qualified Certificate comes from the European Directive on Electronic Signature. In this RFC it describes a certificate whose main purpose is to identify a person with a high level of assurance and which meets the qualification requirements of some applicable legal framework. Deciding whether a certificate counts as qualified under any law is outside the scope of the RFC.

The profile assumes that the issuing CA states that the certificate serves this purpose, that it names a certificate policy consistent with the CA's liabilities, practices and procedures, that it is issued to a living human being, and that the name may be a real name or a pseudonym. The statement of purpose can be given in a certificate policy, in the qualified certificate statements extension, or both.

The distinguished name MUST be unique for each subject certified by one CA, for the whole life time of the CA.
sections.plainLanguage: A qualified certificate is an ID card that says it is a serious one, made for a real person. The rulebook does not say what the law is. It only gives a way to say the card is meant to be that kind.

sections.title: Issuer and Subject Names
sections.content:
The issuer field SHALL identify the organization that issued the certificate, and the name SHOULD be an officially registered one. Its distinguished name uses a subset of domainComponent, countryName, stateOrProvinceName, organizationName, localityName and serialNumber.

The subject field SHALL contain a distinguished name built from a subset of twelve attributes, including commonName, surname, givenName, pseudonym, serialNumber, title and the organization and location attributes. At least one of commonName, givenName or pseudonym SHALL be present.

  • If neither commonName nor pseudonym is present, surname and givenName SHALL be used.
  • pseudonym MUST NOT be combined with surname or givenName.
  • serialNumber tells apart subjects whose names would otherwise be identical, and the CA must make it sufficient to resolve collisions.
  • countryName gives general context and does not have to be the subject's citizenship, residence or the country of issuance.
sections.plainLanguage: Every card must have a name on it, which can be a real name or a nickname. If two people would have the same name, an extra number is added so the cards can be told apart.

sections.title: Extensions Profiled and Added
sections.content:
The profile sets rules for four existing X.509 extensions. If subjectAltName holds a directoryName, it MUST follow the subject naming rules. The certificate policies extension SHALL be present with at least one policy identifier, and it MAY be marked critical. The key usage extension SHALL be present and SHOULD be marked critical; further requirements MAY come from local policy or law.

The subject directory attributes extension MAY carry attributes that are not part of the distinguished name, and MUST NOT be marked critical. Compliant implementations SHALL be able to interpret dateOfBirth, placeOfBirth, gender, countryOfCitizenship and countryOfResidence. A birth date is a GeneralizedTime that SHOULD be noon GMT, for example 19590927120000Z, so that time zones cannot change the date. Gender is "F" or "M" in either case.
sections.plainLanguage: The card can carry extra facts, such as birthday and home country, in a separate box. Dates are written at noon so no one's birthday slips to a different day.

sections.title: Biometric Information
sections.content:
The OPTIONAL biometric information extension stores a hash of a biometric template, not the biometric data itself. Its purpose is to let a relying party authenticate biometric information obtained elsewhere. The extension MAY include a sourceDataUri pointing to the file, which MUST use http:// or https://. The extension MUST NOT be marked critical.

Each entry has a type, a hash algorithm, the hash and the optional URI. Two types are predefined: picture (0) and handwritten-signature (1), and in both cases the hash is calculated over the whole referenced image file. The RFC recommends limiting this to types suitable for human verification, such as an image shown to the relying party. It also warns that checking identifying data can itself be sensitive, so URIs that outsiders cannot easily tie to identities are worth considering.
sections.plainLanguage: The card can hold a fingerprint of a photo, not the photo itself. Anyone who finds the photo can check it matches, because even a tiny change would give a different fingerprint.

sections.title: Qualified Certificate Statements
sections.content:
The OPTIONAL qcStatements extension holds a list of statements. Each has an object identifier and may have a statementInfo parameter whose syntax the identifier defines. The extension may be critical or non-critical, but if critical, all statements in it are critical; mixing is not allowed.

A statement may say that the certificate is issued as a Qualified Certificate under a particular legal system, or relate to the jurisdiction, for example a maximum reliance limit that restricts the CA's liability. Two statements are predefined: id-qcs-pkixQCSyntax-v1 marks conformance with RFC 3039 and MUST NOT be included in certificates issued under this profile, while id-qcs-pkixQCSyntax-v2 marks conformance with this profile.

Both can carry SemanticsInformation, which has an optional semanticsIdentifier OID and optional nameRegistrationAuthorities. When the information is present, at least one of the two fields must be present.
sections.plainLanguage: The card can carry little stamps saying things like "made under version 2 of the rules". Old stamps from the first rulebook are only for recognising old cards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The legal value of a signature checked with a Qualified Certificate depends heavily on the policy governing the private key. Both the key holder and the relying party should make sure the key is used only with the legitimate holder's consent.

Before issuing, a CA should ensure the private key is unique for the subject and under the subject's sole control. It should not issue one if the means of using the key is not protected against unintended use, and it must verify that the public key legitimately represents the subject. Combining the nonRepudiation key usage bit with other bits may have security implications. Comparing names across issuers can mislead, because attribute semantics may differ between issuers. The security considerations of RFC 3280 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: An ID card is only as safe as the secret key behind it. The issuer must check that the key belongs to one person alone, and anyone reading a card should remember that the same name might mean different things at different issuers.
